quick.name: ChatGPT HTML previews
quick.quote: Reported to OpenAI bug bounty 18 October; OpenAI resolved the issue on October 26; browser-side flaw in ChatGPT web frontend; MathLive listener accepted messages without sender check; iframe inserted without sandbox attribute; 'Opening the shared link was the only required action.' OpenAI raised severity P2 to P1. Simon Willison: 'OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty'.
quick.fix: 18 Oct report, 26 Oct fix, listener and iframe are verified. 'Confirmed fixed server-side' is not supported (page describes a browser-side flaw; says only that OpenAI resolved it). 'Nothing for users to do' is not stated; say 'OpenAI says it resolved it on 26 October'. Chain also used a YouTube oEmbed CSP bypass per Willison.

quick.name: Volta infostealer
quick.quote: 'VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim's assets by monetization value.' Posted 31 Oct 2026; sample first seen 2026-10-11. POSTs to OpenRouter, default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6, fails over to kimi-k2 then gemini-2.5-flash if it refuses; runs without the LLM stage if no key. Recommendations: application control on Chrome --headless launches, alert on Chrome --headless from non-developer processes, hardware-backed credential stores; if compromised preserve %APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt, revoke tokens and change passwords.
quick.fix: Reword: Talos says the VOLTA stealer sends a bundle of stolen data about each victim to an LLM (via OpenRouter) to rank that victim's assets by monetization value ('WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' and 'THEIR OPSEC'). It is not ranking victims against each other as stated. The advice 'treat stolen-credential alerts as higher priority' is not in the post; Talos advises blocking or alerting on headless Chrome launched by unknown processes (the ABE decryption path) and using hardware-backed credential stores.

quick.name: Firefox patch gap (Epoch AI)
quick.quote: Report dated October 29, 2026. GLM 5.3 (open-weight, released by Z.ai in August) used published but unshipped fixes plus a separate unpublished vulnerability it rediscovered each time to compromise six Firefox releases (156.0 to 158.0.1); 'it cost only about $1,000 to successfully attack each Firefox version'; fastest attempt about 12 hours; no arbitrary code execution on recent Firefox; no equivalent Chrome exploit after about $100,000; unpublished flaw reported to Mozilla, patched in Firefox 159.0 on October 27. Recommendation: shorten the time fixes are public before reaching users.
quick.fix: Reword: Epoch AI reports GLM 5.3, an open-weight model, built a Firefox attack (local file read from a webpage, not arbitrary code execution) for about $1,000 per version using fixes that were public but not yet shipped, plus a separate unpublished bug now fixed in Firefox 159.0. 'Ship browser updates quickly' is the brief's advice; Epoch's recommendation is for vendors to shrink the gap between publishing a fix and shipping it. Not a pure 'exploits from patches' result.
